name: Tables
description: Learn about Tables and its applications in physics.

content.overview: You've got a pile of numbers from your experiment—now what? Tables are how you organize that mess into something you can actually read. Instead of scattered scribbles, a good table lays everything out so patterns practically jump off the page. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Ever seen a spreadsheet that made your eyes glaze over? That's a table done wrong. Here's what a good data table actually needs:

**1. Clear headers.** The first row tells you what each column is measuring. Something like 'Temperature (°C)', 'Spring Height (mm)', 'Trial Number.'

**2. Units in the headers, not every cell.** Put the unit once, at the top. Saves you space and keeps things tidy.

**3. Organized rows.** Each row = one trial, or one test condition. No mixing things up mid-table.

**4. Consistent decimal places.** If one number has 2 decimals, they all should: 2.50, 3.25, 2.85—not 2.5, 3.25, 2.85. Mixing it up just looks sloppy, even if the numbers are right.

**5. A title.** So when you come back to this table in a week, you actually remember what you were testing.

**Here's the difference in action:**

Bad table:
temp | spring | ???
20 | 15
25 | 18

Good table:
Temperature (°C) | Spring Height (mm)
20 | 15.0
25 | 18.0
30 | 21.5

See it? {{viz:formula-01}} That good table is quietly hiding a pattern—roughly, for every extra 1°C, the spring height creeps up about 0.65 mm. Tables let you spot exactly this kind of trend at a glance. And when there's no pattern at all, that shows up too—which tells you just as much. {{viz:chart-01}}
keyPoints: Clear headers with units, right at the top
Organized by rows—one test per row
Keep your formatting consistent (same decimal places throughout)
Give it a title so you remember what you tested
Line numbers up so patterns are easy to spot
A clean table makes the rest of your analysis so much easier
content.whyItMatters: A messy table hides the very patterns you're trying to find. A clean one practically tells the story of your experiment on its own.
